bib.title: AdaptEvolve: Improving Efficiency of Evolutionary AI Agents through Adaptive Model Selection

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AdaptEvolve: Improving Efficiency of Evolutionary AI Agents through Adaptive Model Selection", Pretam Ray (IIT Kharagpur, work done as an AMD intern), Pratik Prabhanjan Brahma, Zicheng Liu, Emad Barsoum (AMD). arXiv 2602.11931v2, cs.CL. First submitted Feb 2026 (inferred from the arXiv ID); v2 is dated 24 Apr 2026. Venue: preprint. The layout looks ACL-style, but no venue is printed.
COVERAGE: All 9 pages read, 30,112 of 30,112 chars. The references and the appendix (A.1 to A.4, Tables 4 to 7, Figure 2 caption) were included. The extraction is clean text. I did not run the figure-caption script, so Figure 2 and Figure 1 captions come from the text extraction. The paper is short, with no limitations beyond one paragraph.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Confidence-routed model selection inside an evolutionary coding loop cuts compute and keeps most accuracy.
  number: 37.9% average compute reduction, 97.5% of upper-bound accuracy
  setup: OpenEvolve with Qwen3-4B (small) and Qwen3-32B (large), LiveCodeBench v5 and MBPP, 8 iterations, one 8x MI250 node. Cost is a normalized call count, not dollars.
  quote: "reducing total inference cost by an average of37.9% across benchmarks while retaining97.5%of the upper-bound accuracy of static large-model baselines"
  where: abstract, p1
- LiveCodeBench result.
  number: 73.6% vs 75.2% accuracy (97.9%), 34.4% lower cost, efficiency 35.4 vs 23.7 for 32B-only
  setup: Adaptive Hoeffding Tree router, ratio 42:58 small:large, cost 2.08 vs 3.17
  quote: "our method retains97.9%of the 32B upper-bound accuracy (73.6% vs 75.2%) while reducing compute cost by34.4%"
  where: Sec 3.6, p3 (Table 1)
- MBPP result.
  number: 85:15 routing, cost 0.69 vs 1.18 (41.5% cheaper), accuracy 91.3 vs 94.0 (97.1%), efficiency 132.3 vs 79.7
  setup: same models, HAT router
  quote: "the router identifies that 85% of queries are solvable by the small model. This reduces cost by 41.5%while maintaining97.1%of peak accuracy"
  where: p3
- Online adaptation beats a static router because difficulty drifts as the archive fills.
  number: 2.4 points (73.6 vs 71.2) on LiveCodeBench
  setup: Hoeffding Adaptive Tree vs a static Gini decision tree, depth 5, trained on a 50-sample warm-up. The static tree on MBPP gets 82.2 vs HAT 91.3, but at a different ratio (96:04 vs 85:15), so that is not like for like.
  quote: "as the MAP-Elites archive fills with high-scoring solutions, subsequent mutations must address increasingly difficult edge cases, causing the difficulty distribution to shift non-stationary over time"
  where: Sec 2.1, p2
- The learned router beats random routing at the same ratio.
  number: LiveCodeBench 73.6 vs 68.2 (online ratio, 42:58); LLaMA 3.1/HumanEval 74.3 vs 69.4 at 38:62
  setup: LLaMA 3.1 8B and 70B on HumanEval. The speedup is 1.56x vs 70B-only (cost 3.61 vs 4.16).
  quote: "achieving 74.3% accuracy versus 69.4% for random selection, while attaining a 1.56× speedup over the 70B iterative baseline"
  where: Sec 3.6, Table 3, p3
- It beats a cascade (FrugalGPT-style, escalate on failure) at the same accuracy.
  number: efficiency 35.4 vs 26.3; cost 2.08 vs 2.81; accuracy 73.6 vs 73.8
  setup: LiveCodeBench
  quote: "Cascading Baseline (Chen et al., 2023) 36:64 2.81 73.8 26.3 / Adaptive Hoeffding Tree (Ours) 42:58 2.08 73.6 35.4"
  where: Table 2, p3
- Confidence signals separate solved from unsolved small-model generations.
  number: LGC mean 5.858 (unsolved) vs 7.982 (solved); skew 2.044 vs 0.935
  setup: 50-sample warm-up calibration set. The text says gaps of "approximately 1.7 to 2.4 units" (its LGC mean gap is 2.1).
  quote: "LGC shifts from a mean of 5.86 in unsolved cases to 7.98 in solved instances"
  where: A.2, p6
- A nonlinear router beats a linear threshold in a pilot (weak evidence).
  number: accuracy 74.12 vs 70.07; cost 2.02 vs 2.08
  setup: N=50 stratified subset of LiveCodeBench. Random sampling at 35:65 reached 72.23. Prose rounds to 0.70 and 0.74.
  quote: "Decision Tree (Ours) 2.02 74.12 36.7"
  where: Table 5, A.3, p7
- Routing mechanism: a lightweight classifier on the small model's own token-entropy confidence (mean, lowest-group, tail, bottom-K% group) decides whether to keep the small model's mutation or escalate to the large model. Labels come from pass rates of both models (Table 7, p7). Cost is 1 per 32B call and 0.125 per 4B call. The 32B model only keeps being used if it is the only one that solves the problem; otherwise the loop switches back down.

LIMITS
- Authors concede coding-only evaluation. They say it cannot apply to maths or open-ended reasoning, because the loop needs executable code with test pass/fail as fitness.
- Cost is a proxy (parameters x tokens, 32B = 1, 4B = 0.125). They claim token lengths are matched at about 15K and capped at 20,000. Wall-clock agreement is claimed only for LLaMA/HumanEval, and no table for it is given.
- The evolutionary setup is tiny: 8 iterations, population 8, archive 3, 2 islands, seed 42. No variance, seeds or confidence intervals are reported. Qwen3 and LLaMA are the only families.
- The router needs token logprobs, so it does not work on API models that hide them.
- Warm-up labels need ground truth from both models (50 samples). This means a one-off cost that is not counted in the savings.
- The 97.5% and 37.9% averages are over the two Qwen benchmarks (the quoted figures give about 97.5 and about 38 when averaged). The paper does not show the arithmetic.
- The "first" claims are unverified self-assertions. The paper says BEST-Route (Ding et al., 2025) is concurrent work.
- Unclear if HAT's drift detection actually triggered. No drift analysis is shown beyond the accuracy gap.
- Table 1's MBPP baselines differ in ratio from the learned routers, so comparisons there are loose.

BUILDS ON: OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2025), MAP-Elites (Mouret and Clune, 2015), GEAK (Wang et al., 2025); cascades FrugalGPT (Chen et al., 2023); RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2024); big-little speculative decoding (Kim et al., 2023); confidence metrics from "Deep Think with Confidence" (Fu et al., 2025); Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (Bifet and Gavaldà, 2009) via River (Montiel et al., 2021); scikit-learn decision tree (Buitinck et al., 2013).

CODE: none in the paper. The only formula worth keeping is Eq. 1, p2: mutation x'_i = M_S(x_i) if Phi(C(x_i)) = 1, else M_L(x_i). Phi is a binary solvability classifier. Hyperparameters are in Table 6, p7 (max iterations 8, population 8, archive 3, islands 2, temperature 0.6, max tokens 20000).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): the adaptive evolutionary refinement workflow. The small model generates, entropy confidence metrics are computed, a decision-tree router keeps the result or escalates. It is the best one-glance diagram of the router inside the loop.
- Fig 2 (p8 by the extraction, after Table 7): large-model usage (% of calls to 32B) against accuracy on LiveCodeBench. AdaptEvolve gets "near-peak accuracy with only 58% large-model usage", better than the cascade and random. It is the Pareto picture.
- Table 1 (p2-3) holds the main numbers. Table 7 (p7) is the labeling logic for switching.

FIT FOR NOTE 08
- Best fit: note 09 (budgets and cost). The paper's contribution is per-step model allocation inside a loop, with a cost-accuracy Pareto frontier. It adds a concrete figure, 38% cheaper at about 97% accuracy, for routing a small and a large model on confidence.
- Secondary fit: note 08 (as one example of a cost-aware evolutionary loop, with the MAP-Elites archive and the drift point), or note 02 (loop shapes), as the "generate, mutate, select with a router" variant.
- It does not show a loop improving itself over time. The loop's weights, prompts and harness are unchanged, and only model choice varies. It is not evidence for self-improvement as such.
- For the references.md "sharpens" rule, it supports claims that cascades and static routing leave cost on the table. The evidence is narrow: two Qwen3 sizes, coding only, no seeds.

PROBLEMS: Extraction was clean, apart from some collapsed spacing in the tables and equations. Table rows were read from the raw text, and the Table 5 and Table 7 columns may be a little ambiguous. No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. A section on "Cost Metric Validity" refers to Sec 3.6 for wall-clock results, but only the Table 3 speedup is given there. The paper says Table 4 uses "negative entropy" while the metric is defined as negative mean log-prob of top-k, and the appendix also says "values close to 0 indicate model uncertainty", which conflicts with the main text's "High confidence corresponds to peaked distributions". Treat the direction of the metric with caution. Source path: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/04-loop-engineering/sources/ray-2026-adaptevolve.pdf. Note 08's front matter has 27 sources and does not list 2602.11931.
